The earlier NUL-byte file-read hold is resolved by the verified lossless source view, and per-target outcome axes objected to previously are not asserted here (outcome set to cannot_be_determined).

records.reason: Reference [35] identifies this named published Discordant Review, and Methods plus Tables 1–2 show an empirical reassessment of its best-evidence SR-selection finding using original review/constituent-SR information. The interpretation is Cao 2015 and Wu 2015 -> Gurusamy 2013 (original step H, independent step H). It is not merely algorithm reuse. Nevertheless the expert's single generic Methods quotation does not identify this original or prove that target-specific comparison; the earlier exact-target quotation objection remains unresolved. Raw contiguous cells and page regions here document the evidence chain without manufacturing a joined row. This context objection does not exclude the target or reverse the parent's earlier identity/relationship acceptance.

review_selection_comparison_interpretati.basis: Labels, header, and row order within raw page regions. Names and values are interleaved; no complete literal joined row exists. No matching PDF found to independently confirm geometry.
review_selection_comparison_interpretati.confidence: Specific cell associations are an interpretation of the raw text, not a normalized quotation.

source_findings.independent_inspection: Current full raw text read; named review, condition and original-versus-independent selection sequence checked. Table-cell associations remain interpretations, not literal reconstructed quotations.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: A published review-selection finding is empirically reassessed on its documentary inputs; no rerun of original pooled patient estimates or code is reported.
conditional_fact_findings.condition: Parent determines whether that finding/data relationship falls within codebook reproduction scope. A narrower requirement of patient-level reanalysis must not be assumed to exclude a conceptual retest.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: Reference identity, clinical question, selected evidence and separately reported reassessment distinguish this review from the other included reviews. Shared algorithm, topic, overlapping constituent reviews or authors do not collapse independently reported review-selection findings.
conditional_fact_findings.condition: Separate original-report full texts were not supplied; absence is bounded to all shipped and corrected identities supplied here.

actual_limitations: The source front matter is Research Square v3, 28 February 2022, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-1143357/v3; the request work key is 10.20381/ruor-28430. This task has no local proof of repository DOI/version equivalence and does not create an extra original from those versions.
Raw text interleaves columns and spans pages; no PDF geometry newly verified. Literal NULs and missing-glyph placeholders are retained.

The only shipped identity is Bero/Jadad 1997; current original correction maps row 2429 to Bakdach/Hadad 2020, target 0. Neither is reference 35. The selection order alone does not scientifically establish why Bakdach should anchor the row.
Review-selection agreement, algorithm-path agreement and clinical-direction agreement are different facts; no per-target outcome approval is made.
Original selected both Cao 2015 and Wu 2015. Table 3 presents both estimates and a different effect-estimate type for Gurusamy; clinical direction agreement is not numerical reproduction.
expert_reason_corrections: NUL-byte access is now resolved, but it was not the only objection. Setting outcome=cannot_be_determined avoids asserting axes; it does not supply the missing target-specific quotation or resolve finding-scope boundaries.

The expert work identity must be described as the supplied Research Square preprint pending repository/version equivalence, rather than treating the request DOI as verified from the primary front matter.

Read all relevant source sections, Table2 and references, then decide each requested field under the codebook; the previous transport failure is not evidence about the paper.
prior_objections_and_current_corrections.prior_parent_acceptance: Source-access issue resolved with lossless view. Parent checked Methods,Tables1–3,references13/26/6/31–44. Accept reproduction type and21 actual targets;map row2429 to exactBakdach target0 to prevent doublecount. The generic method quote establishes reassessment relationship but not individual outcome axes;those proposed axes withheld conservatively with no thirdcall. Original coding/source unchanged.
prior_objections_and_current_corrections.outcome_objection: All outcome judgments quote the same methods sentence,which does not establish target-specific computation/robustness. Tables show18/21directionsagree although13selectionschange;whether selectionchange materiallyqualifies eachcentralfinding is unsettled. No thirdcall.

expert_opinion.reason: Methods 2.9.1, Table 1, and Table 2 establish that Lunny et al. independently re-ran the Jadad algorithm on the 3 included systematic reviews of Zhao, J.G., J. Wang, and L. Long (2015) [18] (Medicine (Baltimore), 94(26): e1057; listed as Zhao 2015 [18] in Table 1 and Zhao 2015a in Table 2) for Constant score function in surgical versus conservative treatment of displaced midshaft clavicular fractures, selecting the same systematic review (Lenza 2013) at Step H as the original authors. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2429, Bero and Jadad 1997, DOI 10.7326/0003-4819-127-1-199707010-00007) is an uncited methodological guide and was mapped to target_index 0 (Bakdach and Hadad 2020 [13]). Reference [18] is a distinct study from sibling target_index 19 (Zhao, J.G., et al. 2015 [43], Medicine 94(11): e599, on intramedullary nail versus plate fixation for humeral shaft fractures) and target_index 7 (Xu et al. 2017 [34], on intramedullary versus plate fixation for clavicle fractures). The earlier NUL-byte file-read hold is resolved by the verified lossless source view, and per-target outcome axes objected to previously are not asserted here (outcome set to cannot_be_determined).

records.label: objection
records.reason: Reference [30] identifies this named published Discordant Review, and Methods plus Tables 1–2 show an empirical reassessment of its best-evidence SR-selection finding using original review/constituent-SR information. The interpretation is Biau 2006 -> Biau 2006 (original step F, independent step H). It is not merely algorithm reuse. Nevertheless the expert's single generic Methods quotation does not identify this original or prove that target-specific comparison; the earlier exact-target quotation objection remains unresolved. Raw contiguous cells and page regions here document the evidence chain without manufacturing a joined row. This context objection does not exclude the target or reverse the parent's earlier identity/relationship acceptance.

review_selection_comparison_interpretati.basis: Labels, header, and row order within raw page regions. Names and values are interleaved; no complete literal joined row exists. No matching PDF found to independently confirm geometry.
review_selection_comparison_interpretati.confidence: Specific cell associations are an interpretation of the raw text, not a normalized quotation.

source_findings.independent_inspection: Current full raw text read; named review, condition and original-versus-independent selection sequence checked. Table-cell associations remain interpretations, not literal reconstructed quotations.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: A published review-selection finding is empirically reassessed on its documentary inputs; no rerun of original pooled patient estimates or code is reported.
conditional_fact_findings.condition: Parent determines whether that finding/data relationship falls within codebook reproduction scope. A narrower requirement of patient-level reanalysis must not be assumed to exclude a conceptual retest.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: Reference identity, clinical question, selected evidence and separately reported reassessment distinguish this review from the other included reviews. Shared algorithm, topic, overlapping constituent reviews or authors do not collapse independently reported review-selection findings.
conditional_fact_findings.condition: Separate original-report full texts were not supplied; absence is bounded to all shipped and corrected identities supplied here.

actual_limitations: The source front matter is Research Square v3, 28 February 2022, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-1143357/v3; the request work key is 10.20381/ruor-28430. This task has no local proof of repository DOI/version equivalence and does not create an extra original from those versions.
Raw text interleaves columns and spans pages; no PDF geometry newly verified. Literal NULs and missing-glyph placeholders are retained.

The only shipped identity is Bero/Jadad 1997; current original correction maps row 2429 to Bakdach/Hadad 2020, target 0. Neither is reference 30. The selection order alone does not scientifically establish why Bakdach should anchor the row.
Review-selection agreement, algorithm-path agreement and clinical-direction agreement are different facts; no per-target outcome approval is made.
Original Step F versus independent H retain Biau. Discussion says original authors never used the left-side steps D/E/F, conflicting with this Table 2 F entry.

3.3.4 Interpretation of Jadad steps by the Discordant Review author

Overall, there were major differences in the interpretation of the Jadad algorithm across Discordant Review author groups. Several Discordant Reviews (n = 12)

did not implement the Jadad algorithm in sequential steps but rather, used components of the algorithm to assess SRs. In addition, various factors outside the

Jadad algorithm were assessed by half (n = 10/21) Discordant Review authors, including: databases that were searched, the GRADE (Grading of

Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) approach, randomization method, methods used to measure outcomes, measures used to
explore heterogeneity, measures used for establishing comparative superiority or inferiority, statistical approaches used in analyses, presence of subgroup

analyses, software used to perform the analyses, and sources funding.

Most Discordant Reviews (n = 12) used Step I as the �nal decision step of the algorithm. We interpreted Step I to consist of (I1) publication status, (I2) quality

of RCTs, (I3) language restrictions, and (I4) analysis of individual patient data (IPD). We operationalised publication status to be whether SRs included both

published and unpublished (grey literature). In contrast, several Discordant Review authors interpreted this step to consider the date or recency of the review (n 

= 5) or to account for only published literature (n = 3).

The second most common �nal decision step was Step H (n = 5). We interpreted Step H to consist of (H1) search strategies across SRs and (H2) inclusion

criteria and duplicate independent screening of RCTs. Different Interpretations of H1 included: whether the SR was published in a medical journal, and which

electronic databases were searched. Interpretations of H2 included: whether the SR reported publication status and language. Many Discordant Review
authors were not clear in the details of how they interpreted this step. Some Discordant Review authors reported Step H as the �nal decision step but ignored

the criteria for Step G and selected the SR with the highest number of RCTs (n = 2). The rationale behind this decision was not reported.
3.3.4 Time and ease of use in completing Steps H and I of the Jadad assessments

3.3.4.1 Time to do Steps H and I of the Jadad algorithm

Of the 18 Jadad algorithm assessments completed for Steps H and I, the average time was 60 minutes per review (Appendix F and G, Table 1). Ten Jadad

assessments took between 15 minutes and 47.5 minutes with an average of 4.3 SRs to assess (range 3–6). Nine out of the ten were rated as easy to assess,

and one was rated as being moderately di�cult to assess. These nine easy-rated assessments had evaluated Step H of the Jadad algorithm as the �nal

decision step. The moderately rated assessment had evaluated Step I as the �nal decision step.

3.3.4 Interpretation of Jadad steps by the Discordant Review author

Overall, there were major differences in the interpretation of the Jadad algorithm across Discordant Review author groups. Several Discordant Reviews (n = 12)

did not implement the Jadad algorithm in sequential steps but rather, used components of the algorithm to assess SRs. In addition, various factors outside the

Jadad algorithm were assessed by half (n = 10/21) Discordant Review authors, including: databases that were searched, the GRADE (Grading of

Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) approach, randomization method, methods used to measure outcomes, measures used to
explore heterogeneity, measures used for establishing comparative superiority or inferiority, statistical approaches used in analyses, presence of subgroup

analyses, software used to perform the analyses, and sources funding.

Most Discordant Reviews (n = 12) used Step I as the �nal decision step of the algorithm. We interpreted Step I to consist of (I1) publication status, (I2) quality

of RCTs, (I3) language restrictions, and (I4) analysis of individual patient data (IPD). We operationalised publication status to be whether SRs included both

published and unpublished (grey literature). In contrast, several Discordant Review authors interpreted this step to consider the date or recency of the review (n 

= 5) or to account for only published literature (n = 3).

The second most common �nal decision step was Step H (n = 5). We interpreted Step H to consist of (H1) search strategies across SRs and (H2) inclusion

criteria and duplicate independent screening of RCTs. Different Interpretations of H1 included: whether the SR was published in a medical journal, and which

electronic databases were searched. Interpretations of H2 included: whether the SR reported publication status and language. Many Discordant Review
authors were not clear in the details of how they interpreted this step. Some Discordant Review authors reported Step H as the �nal decision step but ignored

the criteria for Step G and selected the SR with the highest number of RCTs (n = 2). The rationale behind this decision was not reported.
3.3.4 Time and ease of use in completing Steps H and I of the Jadad assessments

3.3.4.1 Time to do Steps H and I of the Jadad algorithm

Of the 18 Jadad algorithm assessments completed for Steps H and I, the average time was 60 minutes per review (Appendix F and G, Table 1). Ten Jadad

assessments took between 15 minutes and 47.5 minutes with an average of 4.3 SRs to assess (range 3–6). Nine out of the ten were rated as easy to assess,

and one was rated as being moderately di�cult to assess. These nine easy-rated assessments had evaluated Step H of the Jadad algorithm as the �nal

decision step. The moderately rated assessment had evaluated Step I as the �nal decision step.
3.3.4.1 Ease of use rating for �nal decision Steps H and I of the Jadad algorithm

Of the 18 Jadad assessments we completed with �nal decision for Steps H and Step I, the median ease rating was easy (Appendix F and G, Table 1). Ten out

of 18 (56%) assessments were rated easy, six (33%) were rated moderate, one moderate/hard (6%), and one hard (6%). All the assessments rated as easy were

based on completing Step H. Of the easy assessments, the average number of SRs to assess was 4.4 (range 3–6 SRs). Of the eight moderate to hard

records.label: objection
records.reason: Reference [39] identifies this named published Discordant Review, and Methods plus Tables 1–2 show an empirical reassessment of its best-evidence SR-selection finding using original review/constituent-SR information. The interpretation is Riboh 2014 -> Chan 2014 (original step I, independent step H). It is not merely algorithm reuse. Nevertheless the expert's single generic Methods quotation does not identify this original or prove that target-specific comparison; the earlier exact-target quotation objection remains unresolved. Raw contiguous cells and page regions here document the evidence chain without manufacturing a joined row. This context objection does not exclude the target or reverse the parent's earlier identity/relationship acceptance.

review_selection_comparison_interpretati.primary_outcome_and_intervention: range of motion; early/delayed rehabilitation after rotator cuff repair
review_selection_comparison_interpretati.basis: Labels, header, and row order within raw page regions. Names and values are interleaved; no complete literal joined row exists. No matching PDF found to independently confirm geometry.
review_selection_comparison_interpretati.confidence: Specific cell associations are an interpretation of the raw text, not a normalized quotation.

source_findings.independent_inspection: Current full raw text read; named review, condition and original-versus-independent selection sequence checked. Table-cell associations remain interpretations, not literal reconstructed quotations.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: A published review-selection finding is empirically reassessed on its documentary inputs; no rerun of original pooled patient estimates or code is reported.
conditional_fact_findings.condition: Parent determines whether that finding/data relationship falls within codebook reproduction scope. A narrower requirement of patient-level reanalysis must not be assumed to exclude a conceptual retest.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: Reference identity, clinical question, selected evidence and separately reported reassessment distinguish this review from the other included reviews. 3.3.2 Frequency of agreement and disagreement in systematic review �ndings

Ten out of 13 (77%) discordant Jadad assessments led to agreement in the �ndings (direction of effect was the same) (Table 3). The remaining three

independent Jadad assessments that disagreed led to a different direction of the effect estimates.

Overall, 18 out of the 21 (86%) independent Jadad assessments agreed in direction of the �ndings despite 13 having chosen a different SR. We present a case

study in Appendix E to illustrate a case study of the clinical impact of choosing one SR using the Jadad algorithm.
3.3.3 Cochrane versus non-Cochrane reviews chosen

Of the 21 Jadad assessments, four Cochrane reviews were chosen either by us or the Discordant Review authors (Table 3). On four occasions we chose a

Cochrane review, and twice the Discordant Review authors chose a Cochrane review.

(2019) [41] (listed as Zhiyong 2019 in Tables 1–3) on unilateral versus bilateral balloon kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures using short-term VAS pain scores, finding that independent Jadad reassessment selected Feng 2015 (favourable effect) via Step I rather than the original authors' selection of Sun et al. 2016 (null effect) via Step I (Table 2, Table 3). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2429, Bero & Jadad 1997, 10.7326/0003-4819-127-1-199707010-00007) is an uncited 1997 guidance paper mapped to target_index 0, and Cui Zhiyong et al. (2019) [41] (Pain Physician 2019; 22: 15-28) is an independent Discordant Review by a different author group from Xiaofeng Chen et al. (2018) [33] (target_index 6) and Tan et al. (2018) [36] (target_index 12), each separately reassessed in Tables 1–3. Prior source-access and outcome-scope objections are addressed via the lossless source view and by setting outcome to cannot_be_determined.

3.3.4 Interpretation of Jadad steps by the Discordant Review author

Overall, there were major differences in the interpretation of the Jadad algorithm across Discordant Review author groups. Several Discordant Reviews (n = 12)

did not implement the Jadad algorithm in sequential steps but rather, used components of the algorithm to assess SRs. In addition, various factors outside the

Jadad algorithm were assessed by half (n = 10/21) Discordant Review authors, including: databases that were searched, the GRADE (Grading of

Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) approach, randomization method, methods used to measure outcomes, measures used to
explore heterogeneity, measures used for establishing comparative superiority or inferiority, statistical approaches used in analyses, presence of subgroup

analyses, software used to perform the analyses, and sources funding.

Most Discordant Reviews (n = 12) used Step I as the �nal decision step of the algorithm. We interpreted Step I to consist of (I1) publication status, (I2) quality

of RCTs, (I3) language restrictions, and (I4) analysis of individual patient data (IPD). We operationalised publication status to be whether SRs included both

published and unpublished (grey literature). In contrast, several Discordant Review authors interpreted this step to consider the date or recency of the review (n 

= 5) or to account for only published literature (n = 3).

The second most common �nal decision step was Step H (n = 5). We interpreted Step H to consist of (H1) search strategies across SRs and (H2) inclusion

criteria and duplicate independent screening of RCTs. Different Interpretations of H1 included: whether the SR was published in a medical journal, and which

electronic databases were searched. Interpretations of H2 included: whether the SR reported publication status and language. Many Discordant Review
authors were not clear in the details of how they interpreted this step. Some Discordant Review authors reported Step H as the �nal decision step but ignored

the criteria for Step G and selected the SR with the highest number of RCTs (n = 2). The rationale behind this decision was not reported.

3.3.4.1 Time to do Steps H and I of the Jadad algorithm

Of the 18 Jadad algorithm assessments completed for Steps H and I, the average time was 60 minutes per review (Appendix F and G, Table 1). Ten Jadad

assessments took between 15 minutes and 47.5 minutes with an average of 4.3 SRs to assess (range 3–6). Nine out of the ten were rated as easy to assess,

and one was rated as being moderately di�cult to assess. These nine easy-rated assessments had evaluated Step H of the Jadad algorithm as the �nal

decision step. The moderately rated assessment had evaluated Step I as the �nal decision step.

3.3.2 Frequency of agreement and disagreement in systematic review �ndings

Ten out of 13 (77%) discordant Jadad assessments led to agreement in the �ndings (direction of effect was the same) (Table 3). The remaining three

independent Jadad assessments that disagreed led to a different direction of the effect estimates.

Overall, 18 out of the 21 (86%) independent Jadad assessments agreed in direction of the �ndings despite 13 having chosen a different SR. We present a case

study in Appendix E to illustrate a case study of the clinical impact of choosing one SR using the Jadad algorithm.
3.3.3 Cochrane versus non-Cochrane reviews chosen

Of the 21 Jadad assessments, four Cochrane reviews were chosen either by us or the Discordant Review authors (Table 3). On four occasions we chose a

Cochrane review, and twice the Discordant Review authors chose a Cochrane review.

records.label: objection
records.reason: Reference [42] identifies this named published Discordant Review, and Methods plus Tables 1–2 show an empirical reassessment of its best-evidence SR-selection finding using original review/constituent-SR information. The interpretation is Rabi et al 2015 -> Handoll 2012 (original step H, independent step H). It is not merely algorithm reuse. Nevertheless the expert's single generic Methods quotation does not identify this original or prove that target-specific comparison; the earlier exact-target quotation objection remains unresolved. Raw contiguous cells and page regions here document the evidence chain without manufacturing a joined row. This context objection does not exclude the target or reverse the parent's earlier identity/relationship acceptance.

review_selection_comparison_interpretati.basis: Labels, header, and row order within raw page regions. Names and values are interleaved; no complete literal joined row exists. No matching PDF found to independently confirm geometry.
review_selection_comparison_interpretati.confidence: Specific cell associations are an interpretation of the raw text, not a normalized quotation.

source_findings.independent_inspection: Current full raw text read; named review, condition and original-versus-independent selection sequence checked. Table-cell associations remain interpretations, not literal reconstructed quotations.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: A published review-selection finding is empirically reassessed on its documentary inputs; no rerun of original pooled patient estimates or code is reported.
conditional_fact_findings.condition: Parent determines whether that finding/data relationship falls within codebook reproduction scope. A narrower requirement of patient-level reanalysis must not be assumed to exclude a conceptual retest.

conditional_fact_findings.finding: Reference identity, clinical question, selected evidence and separately reported reassessment distinguish this review from the other included reviews. Shared algorithm, topic, overlapping constituent reviews or authors do not collapse independently reported review-selection findings.
conditional_fact_findings.condition: Separate original-report full texts were not supplied; absence is bounded to all shipped and corrected identities supplied here.

actual_limitations: The source front matter is Research Square v3, 28 February 2022, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-1143357/v3; the request work key is 10.20381/ruor-28430. This task has no local proof of repository DOI/version equivalence and does not create an extra original from those versions.
Raw text interleaves columns and spans pages; no PDF geometry newly verified. Literal NULs and missing-glyph placeholders are retained.

The only shipped identity is Bero/Jadad 1997; current original correction maps row 2429 to Bakdach/Hadad 2020, target 0. Neither is reference 42. The selection order alone does not scientifically establish why Bakdach should anchor the row.
Review-selection agreement, algorithm-path agreement and clinical-direction agreement are different facts; no per-target outcome approval is made.
expert_reason_corrections: NUL-byte access is now resolved, but it was not the only objection. Setting outcome=cannot_be_determined avoids asserting axes; it does not supply the missing target-specific quotation or resolve finding-scope boundaries.

3.3.4 Interpretation of Jadad steps by the Discordant Review author

Overall, there were major differences in the interpretation of the Jadad algorithm across Discordant Review author groups. Several Discordant Reviews (n = 12)

did not implement the Jadad algorithm in sequential steps but rather, used components of the algorithm to assess SRs. In addition, various factors outside the

Jadad algorithm were assessed by half (n = 10/21) Discordant Review authors, including: databases that were searched, the GRADE (Grading of

Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) approach, randomization method, methods used to measure outcomes, measures used to
explore heterogeneity, measures used for establishing comparative superiority or inferiority, statistical approaches used in analyses, presence of subgroup

analyses, software used to perform the analyses, and sources funding.

Most Discordant Reviews (n = 12) used Step I as the �nal decision step of the algorithm. We interpreted Step I to consist of (I1) publication status, (I2) quality

of RCTs, (I3) language restrictions, and (I4) analysis of individual patient data (IPD). We operationalised publication status to be whether SRs included both

published and unpublished (grey literature). In contrast, several Discordant Review authors interpreted this step to consider the date or recency of the review (n 

= 5) or to account for only published literature (n = 3).

The second most common �nal decision step was Step H (n = 5). We interpreted Step H to consist of (H1) search strategies across SRs and (H2) inclusion

criteria and duplicate independent screening of RCTs. Different Interpretations of H1 included: whether the SR was published in a medical journal, and which

electronic databases were searched. Interpretations of H2 included: whether the SR reported publication status and language. Many Discordant Review
authors were not clear in the details of how they interpreted this step. Some Discordant Review authors reported Step H as the �nal decision step but ignored

the criteria for Step G and selected the SR with the highest number of RCTs (n = 2). The rationale behind this decision was not reported.
3.3.4 Time and ease of use in completing Steps H and I of the Jadad assessments

3.3.4.1 Time to do Steps H and I of the Jadad algorithm

Of the 18 Jadad algorithm assessments completed for Steps H and I, the average time was 60 minutes per review (Appendix F and G, Table 1). Ten Jadad

assessments took between 15 minutes and 47.5 minutes with an average of 4.3 SRs to assess (range 3–6). Nine out of the ten were rated as easy to assess,

and one was rated as being moderately di�cult to assess. These nine easy-rated assessments had evaluated Step H of the Jadad algorithm as the �nal

decision step. The moderately rated assessment had evaluated Step I as the �nal decision step.
3.3.4.1 Ease of use rating for �nal decision Steps H and I of the Jadad algorithm

Of the 18 Jadad assessments we completed with �nal decision for Steps H and Step I, the median ease rating was easy (Appendix F and G, Table 1). Ten out

of 18 (56%) assessments were rated easy, six (33%) were rated moderate, one moderate/hard (6%), and one hard (6%). All the assessments rated as easy were

source_evidence.quote:
rs1324183 in
MPDZ-NF1B
was reported to be associated with keratoconus [
23
,
24
,
30
,
31
]. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood of all participants using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA concentration was inspected by Nanodrop 2000 (Thermo Fisher, USA). The target sequence which contained the rs1324183 site (Primers, forward: 5’-TCCTACCAGCTTGTCTCCAAA-3’, reverse: 5’-ACAAGAAGCCACAAGTCTGGC-3’) were amplified by ordinary PCR (Allsheng, Hangzhou, China) and then conducted Sanger sequencing on ABI 3730 analyzer (Applied, Biosystem). Sites of variation were identified through a comparison of DNA sequences with the corresponding GenBank reference sequences using the Mutation Surveyor software, version 5.0.0. Genotyping (Heterozygous mutation, homozygous mutation and wild-type) were classified based on the results of Sanger sequencing.

and

source_evidence.quote:
In this study, we assessed the replication correlation between SNP rs1324183 and keratoconus in our northwestern population of China, which have never been confirmed in such population. SNP rs1324183 (
MPDZ-NFIB,
chr9:13,557,491) was first screened associated with the central corneal thickness (CCT) in an Asian cohort in 2012 [
32
], and then was studied in different KC population in the world [
23
,
24
,
30
,
31
,
33
]. They found that SNP rs1324183 was significantly associated with KC (p < 0.05), conferring a high risk towards KC, and should be used as genetic markers for the diagnosis of keratoconus in the future. In our study, similarly, we also obtained the close correlation between SNP rs1324183 and KC, in particular, the allele A and the genotype AA of rs1324183 (
MPDZ-NFIB
) were both confirmed as higher risks for keratoconus in our population (Tables
1
and
2
). However, we did not find any differences in gender and age between our KC cases and controls (Table
1
). Results concerning gender and age preponderance on keratoconus vary between previous studies. Most of them demonstrated that gender and age both associated with high prevalence of KC [
34
–
40
], but some people reported that there was no gender preponderance in KC and also no significant association between age and the prevalence of KC [
11
,
41
]. In our study, no difference in gender and age between KC cases and controls could be because of the small number of subjects.

source_evidence.quote: The good-enough level (GEL) model posits that the rate of change in psychotherapy is related to the total dose of therapy. The psychotherapy dose-response literature has typically measured dose as number of sessions attended without considering the number of days or weeks it takes to complete the sessions (session frequency). The current study sought to replicate the GEL model and explore if session frequency moderates the influence that the number of sessions has on the rate of change in psychotherapy. An archived naturalistic data set with a US university counseling center sample (n=1,207), with treatment progress measured using the Outcome Questionnaire-45 (Lambert et al., 1996), was used. Our results are consistent with the GEL model (i.e., clients who attended fewer sessions evidenced faster rates of change), but extended it by showing that the rate of change was also influenced by session frequency (i.e., clients who attended more sessions on average per week demonstrated more rapid improvement). Evidence suggests that clinicians and researchers should give consideration to session frequency, both in their work with clients and how "dose" is operationalized in psychotherapy research.

source_evidence.quote: A1 Where IS scholars publish: Small replication Dean, Lowry and Humpherys (2011) used the 19-year period 1990-2008; we used the ten-year period 2006-2015.9 Whereas their sample included all Carnegie research categories, we included only the most research active (“very high”) level. Our sample of 67 promoted scholars is thus smaller than their sample of 210. We classified the promoted professors’ publications to compare them with Lowry et al.: all journals that they did not consider, the eight they included from the Basket, the 13 that they included as other high-level journals dedicated to IS, and the 119 journals that they considered for inclusion but decided to exclude from comparison with the Basket. The modal reason for exclusions was a provenance “primarily” in another discipline, with 55 excluded on this basis, 28 from CS and 10 from Management or OB/Management. By the latter, they meant Organization Science and Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes. We distinguished between exclusions based on discipline from the other reasons, and noted journals that were not considered at all for inclusion by Lowry et al. We also followed Dean et al. by classifying journals as business (not IS) and as CS and Engineering. For this purpose, we used the ISI classifications found in Journal Citation Reports. These classifications are widely used in bibliometric studies despite recognized limitations (Rafols & Leydesdorff, 2009; Zhang, Liu, Janssens, Liang, & Glänzel, 2010). 9 Some of our data include early 2016 as well. We made one exception about business schools, including one scholar with a specific “IS” designation in the Heinz College of Information Systems, Public Policy and Management of Carnegie Mellon. This scholar focuses on medical informatics. Volume 4 Paper 12 26 Does “Evaluating Journal Quality and the AIS Senior Scholars Journal Basket…” Support the Basket? We find them to have face validity in the present usage. The 67 scholars are those with data on publications on their university website who were promoted to Associate Professor in the last decade in one of the 115 “highest research activity” universities in the Carnegie classification. Our results are very close to those in Dean et al. (2011). They found that promoted IS scholars published 23% of their articles in CS and Engineering journals; we find 24%. They found 22% of articles in non-IS business journals; we find 21%. Comparing our results with the 21 IS journals examined in Lowry et al., we find that the promoted scholars averaged about five articles in included journals, four in explicitly excluded journals, and four and a half in non-considered journals. Our findings could be interpreted as consistent with the prescriptions in Lowry et al., as almost one quarter of the articles appeared in Basket journals. source_evidence.quote:
People leniently interpret sentences from second-language accented and language disordered speakers: a replication and extension
Peiyao Chen; Heather Chau; Scott R. Schroeder
ABSTRACT
Prior evidence suggests that listeners leniently interpret sentences with errors when they are produced by a second-language speaker. Here, we aim to replicate this lenient listener effect for second-language speakers, and to determine whether this effect extends to speakers with a language disorder. 483 English native speakers listened to sentences and answered comprehension questions. A subset of sentences was implausible due to an error (e.g. “The mother gave the candle the daughter”). When answering the comprehension question, a non-literal answer reflected listeners’ leniency. We found that listeners were more likely to interpret implausible sentences non-literally when they were produced by second-language accented and language disordered speakers. The results replicate the lenient listener effect for second-language speakers and extend it to language disordered speakers. These results suggest that listeners employ a different, less literal comprehension strategy when listening to second-language and language disordered speakers, which could affect social interactions.
